utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Sarapa. Further cross-examination by Mr. Sarapa: [Interpretation]:

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would like to clarify in which year they were slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, they were slaughtered in early 1995. We never moved them to the newly-built pigsty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last comment again? We heard no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Thank you. I think that this has been resolved. However, I just received notice concerning the cherry trees. Something was not recorded in the transcript; namely, that there were never any cherry trees grown on the land which was given to the army for its use. Could we clarify this as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that a matter of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This relates to the transcript, an error in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Mr. President, I think the question was -- was answered at page 44, line 5, at the military farm land there were no fruit trees whatsoever, and he went on to describe other fruit trees located elsewhere. I think the question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The issue may be that -- whether the witness had specifically said that there were -- there had been no cherry trees. Did you say that, Mr. Lakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that there were no cherry trees whatsoever. I have lived there for 30 years. In this portion here where the stables are, that used to be an orchard which belonged to the German settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Lakic. That concludes your testimony, and I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have a slightly modified tender list. We have P02103 -- I'm sorry, yeah - thank you - we have PIC 0093, which is page 212 of P02103. That was marked by the witness just now during his redirect examination. We have PIC 00092, which is a marked version by the witness during his redirect examination of Defence Exhibit 7D00364. Mr. President, we would also tender P02506, which is the Zvornik Brigade order assigning the witness to be the manager of the military farm. That was also shown to him during his redirect examination. That is now in e-court. For the record, the ERN on that is 0073-3281 to 0073-3281. That's the B/C/S. The English translation is at 0086-1117 to 0086-1117. Finally, we would offer P02505, which is the map of this area brought by the witness himself and marked prior to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Would there be any objection on -- from the Defence? Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not really objection. I can't see what purpose there is in putting in the map that -- a very small portion of which we saw on the ELMO. It's a map of the land as it is now. It was pre-marked by the witness before he came into court. And the whole of the map has not been used in these proceedings and has not even been seen by the accused or any of us. We only saw a rather small portion of it. And it seems to me that the witness now having dealt with a scale map of the whole relevant area and marked and signed it in the course of the proceedings, that is a rather better piece of evidence to -- for the Trial Chamber to rely on in coming to any decision. The -- the modern map on the ELMO seemed to me to be very little evidential value at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're talking about P02505?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To the contrary, Mr. President, the map brought in by the witness himself and marked by the witness is of high probative value. My learned friends have had the entire map in hard copy. It was here. It is pretty much repeated by the exhibit that my learned friend wants to tender and basically repeated the direct testimony, and so I think both are probative. You could see that I actually asked the witness to mark something on my learned friend's exhibit as well, but I think altogether they are useful for the Court to illustrate where these areas were, and they've had -- they have the entire map that was used, just as the portions of other maps are used, that's no reason to exclude introducing a map into evidence. I don't think we need to establish a precedent of using an entire map before it's introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't see this objection as a real objection, as Mr. Haynes stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I mean, I've got the reply. I was inviting the Prosecution to be economical with the sort of evidence you've got to consider and sensible about what is probative and what has properly been dealt with during the course of evidence, but apparently they want to put in this map, so: So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit them, and it is for the Chamber to assess the weight of any map at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I come to a second document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The document that was shown to the witness in re-examination, the order assigning him his duties as a member of the 1st Battalion has no 65 ter number, as I understand it. It was not served upon us as a document that was going to be used with this witness, notwithstanding the fact it was shown to him during proofing, and although it is now in e-court, the English version has not been shown to the Court. I've got a copy of the English version, and crucially, of course, in the -- yes, thank you. Crucially, I would like to place on the record that in the English version, the assignment is of him as manager of an army farm, not the military farm, as was stated in its introduction into evidence just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that in B/C/S, it's Vojna Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Which is army, of course. I make the principled objection that there is no 65 ter number, but I accept that it's a document that probably was properly used in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is not an objection either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You heard what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And having said that -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to note at this moment that the Chamber had a ruling earlier on that the fact that a document has not a 65 number does not prohibit it from being admitted. Having said that and having noted the statement by Mr. Haynes, the Chamber will admit them all. Mr. Haynes, you have some documents? Mr. Sarapa or Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll deal with it. I propose to -- I propose to seek to admit into evidence two documents. They're 7D364, which is the plan of the farm in its original and unmarked form. The advantage being, of course, in that form you can zoom in and zoom out, so I would suggest that it's appropriate that that goes into evidence. Because we broke in the middle of the witness's evidence, the document that he marked has been saved under two numbers, 7DIC 90, which is the document number saved at the break, and 7DIC 91, the document saved at the end of his testimony, and signed and dated by him. I don't seek to put into evidence the document saved at the break, the partially marked document, but only 7DIC 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. No opposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They are so admitted. Any preliminaries? Any administrative matters? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I mentioned briefly, we had e-mailed the -- we e-mailed court officers last night. As you know, it's not our habit to e-mail the Chambers directly or the Judges directly. We -- there was an accelerated pace, and I'm sure you've noticed, of the witnesses, and we, up until last night, were trying to bring in people to meet that accelerated pace. We unfortunately were not able to, based on a number of the usual problems with the witnesses' schedules, visa -- changing visas, this kind of thing. Just to show you where we got into trouble, and this is not meant as a criticism to anybody because we appreciate the targeted cross-examinations, but the estimates that we were partially basing our estimates on were the problem. The Prosecution estimated five hours, and our actual was four hours and 45 minutes. That's partly due to luck. Some witnesses went over and some witnesses went under, but the Defence total estimate was 12 and a half hours, and their actual was five and a half hours. That left us seven hours. We built in a one-day insurance policy, when it turned into two days, that's where we ran into the problem. I am going to work with the victim witness to try to bring this into a two-day insurance policy. We did that before the break, and we had people stacked up here for two weeks, but I just don't know any other way to do it. And I understand the Defence has to estimate how long our direct will be, and then they have to estimate what their other colleagues are going to -- how long they are going to be, so their estimates -- they are in a very difficult position to estimate. So, as I say, it is not meant as a criticism but this is what we base our -- as best we can, on our estimate. So this is the problem we find ourselves in. And I will try to make sure it doesn't happen again, but it's just, as you can tell, difficult. I do have some handouts on another topic which I -- which will explain to Court and counsel some of the witnesses we intend to -- to ask for withdrawal and our estimates of future witness time, if the Court would like to take time to do that. I've got copies for people here. If you want to do that in open court or we can -- it can be handed out and people can see it after court. It all is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we can be handed over, those copies right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could get some help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But no discussion today. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, for your statement, and I would recommend very much to the parties to have dialogues for mutual cooperation in updating the estimates, et cetera. So noting there is no further administrative matters, the hearing is now adjourned until -- Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. While technically it's not an administrative matter, but I was asked by my client as well as other co-accused in this case to raise one issue before the Trial Chamber. It has to do with their transportation back to the Detention Unit. It is obvious that we are going to adjourn earlier today, just as it was the situation yesterday, and the transportation of all the accused happens hours after we adjourn. So they spend two, sometimes three hours, in these small cells without any comfort, without possibility to use toilet and everything, and they feel very uncomfortable about this. So if the Trial Chamber can assist us in a situation like this and ask the Registry to organise their transportation back to the Detention Unit as soon as practical after we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thank you, but my understanding is that the transportation is partly -- is falling on the purview of the Dutch police, not by the security guards. I think that's the problem, but I will look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was also informed that in addition to that matter, the Dutch police is in charge of transporting the other group of accused, and there is some problem. But I will ask the registry to look into the matter, whether there can be some improvement. Having said that, we are adjourned until Monday morning, and I hope everybody will have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
